## Last week: where we left off {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **The panic** (Cambridge Analytica/Brexit) about platforms as mind-control machines does not survive contact with the effects literature — persuasion effects are small, voters are not dupes.
- **The reality** (Kreiss & McGregor): platforms are **active agents** in campaigns — partisan firm teams, quasi-digital consulting, industrial-scale ad optimisation — not neutral pipes.
- The takeaway was **infrastructural, not hypnotic** influence: platforms shape what campaigns *can do*, without hacking anyone's mind.
:::

## Today's running question {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
### Leg 2 of the semester's verdict
Does digital media strengthen or weaken democratic institutions? Today we test this by asking: **does lowering the cost of political participation close the gap between the engaged and the disengaged — or does it just give the already-engaged one more advantage?**
:::

Today's class (Ch 7):

- Meet the **four ages of campaigning** — and how platforms extend, rather than replace, what came before.
- Ask whether platforms actually **decide election outcomes** (spoiler: rarely, alone).
- Unpack platform campaign strategies: **attention & interaction, persuasion, mobilisation & demobilisation**.
- Read Heiss & Matthes [-@heissMatthesDoesIncidental2019] on whether **incidental exposure** to political content equalises or reinforces the gap between the politically interested and disengaged.
- Case: an Austrian two-wave panel study around the 2017 national election.

## Case: the Bird of the Year scandal {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- November 2020: New Zealand's **Bird of the Year** contest — a genuinely popular annual vote (55,000+ voters, celebrity endorsements) — was hit by **1,500 fraudulent ballots** from fake emails, all from the same IP address.
- The **Kākāpō** ("fat, flightless" parrot) won; furious fans called it a "stolen election."
- 2019: suspected "Russian meddling" turned out to be legitimate votes from Russian bird lovers.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### Why the textbook opens Ch 7 with this
Even a *bird contest* needs legitimate, trusted procedures to produce results people accept — and campaigning is **affective and emotional**, not just informational, whatever is being contested [@klingerPlatformsPowerPolitics2023, Ch 7].
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Elections matter because they let people **replace rulers without violence** — but that only works if losers accept the result. This is why "the election was stolen" claims, however trivial the contest, are corrosive.
:::

## The four ages of campaigning {.smaller}

| Era | Roughly when | Logic |
|---|---|---|
| **Party-centred** | Late 1800s–1950s | Strong party apparatus plans everything; social identity of party membership matters more than ideology |
| **Mass-media-centred** | 1950s–1970s | Parties adapt to TV's logic — sound bites, polling, "mediatization" |
| **Target-group-centred** | 1970s–1990s | Cable TV + early Internet enable "narrowcasting" to predefined groups (partisanship, geography, race) |
| **Individual-centred** | 2008–present | Platforms enable **data-driven, personalised** micro-targeting of individual voters |

---

::: {.callout-tip}
No era fully replaces the last — parties still doorknock and print T-shirts. Each new era **adds** tools and logics on top of the old ones.
:::

::: {.center}
![](../img/week-07-doorknocking-chandler-mather.webp){width="45%"}
:::

Max Chandler-Mather doorknocking in his Brisbane electorate, 2024. Greens MPs and volunteers have become synonymous with doorknocking and field work in recent years. ## Individual-centred campaigning, in detail {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Campaigns mine **public, party, and commercial data** — plus platform behavioural data — to score individual voters' probability of voting and their issue positions.
- Ads are **micro-targeted** to scored groups, not broad demographic categories.
- **"A/B testing on steroids"**: campaigns run thousands of message variants and adjust based on what performs (Ch 6's Trump example: up to 175,000 ad variants in one day).
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### Two subtypes [@rommeleGibsonScientificSubversive2020]
- **Scientific**: data science, algorithms, machine learning as an integrated strategy.
- **Subversive**: disinformation, weaponising social media *against* mass media, embracing foreign interference.
:::
:::
:::

## Do platforms decide who wins? {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
### The textbook's answer: rarely, alone
"Elections are not won or lost on social media." Obama 2008 and Trump 2016 both used platforms skilfully — but the economy, party coalitions, incumbency, and the fractured state of the opposing party mattered just as much, if not more.
:::

- Social media can **equalise resources** between well-funded and under-resourced candidates — low barriers to entry, potential for large reach.
- But well-established parties with deep pockets can *also* out-invest challengers in digital expertise and data.
- **Schradie** [-@schradieRevolutionThatWasnt2019]: ideology, class, resources, organisation, and skills shape who actually benefits from "free" digital tools — comparatively **older forms of power persist** even as the technology looks revolutionary.
- Her North Carolina case study of labour and Tea Party activists finds a **"digital activism gap"**: better-funded, more hierarchical organisations — often the conservative ones — sustain the *routine, paid-staff labour* digital production actually requires, while resource-poor, horizontally organised progressive groups burn out despite genuinely embracing participatory digital culture.

# Platform campaign strategies

## Attention and interaction {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Early campaign websites were **one-way, broadcast** channels. Interactivity crept in through the 2000s.
- Despite the *potential* for dialogue, research consistently finds **more broadcasting than genuine interaction** — campaigns have clear, narrow goals (votes, volunteers, funds) and interacting at scale is resource-intensive.
- Parties construct **"authenticity illusions"** [@klingerPlatformsPowerPolitics2023, Ch 7] — staged-but-convincing self-presentation — because audiences expect candidates to seem "real."
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### Not inevitable
Austria took until **2013** for all parties to use social media — driven less by strategy than by fear of ridicule for *not* being on Twitter/Facebook.
:::
:::
:::

## What is an "authenticity illusion"? {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note}
### Enli's [-@enliTrustMeAuthentic2015] concept
Political actors deliberately deploy markers of **spontaneity** and **amateurism** — the visual/verbal signals audiences associate with "unscripted" — inside content that is, in fact, planned and produced. The illusion isn't lying; it's borrowing the *aesthetic* of authenticity.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Spontaneity markers**

- Live or live-looking video (Instagram/TikTok "stories" over polished ads)
- Casual, in-the-moment framing — a kitchen, a car, a doorstep
- Apparent mistakes or asides left in, signalling "this wasn't rehearsed"
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Amateurism markers**

- Handheld, lower-fidelity footage instead of studio production
- Selfie angles, informal language, deliberately "rough" editing
- A famous example: Obama's campaign signed tweets **he personally wrote** "-bo" — distinguishing them from staff-drafted ones, so the *authentic* tweets could be told apart from the professionally managed account
:::
:::

---

::: {.callout-important}
### Why it matters for this unit
This is the same move as the Norway "We are more than numbers" case (Ch 6): platforms reward content that **looks** personal and unmediated — so professionalised campaigns learn to perform informality, which is itself a strategic, resourced skill, not the absence of one.
:::

For example, let's check [this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5G2xDe-h-H0) released by Mamdani to show that his videos were authentic and not AI generated.  




## Persuasion: harder than it looks {.smaller}

- Partisanship, ideology and identity are **stable**, formed through long socialisation — short campaigns rarely flip them.
- What campaigns *can* shift, short-term: which **issues and identities feel salient** right now.
- Social media is potent here because it **blends mass messaging with social diffusion** — political content arrives from friends and weak ties, not just ads, which makes it more trusted (even though most people distrust platforms and political ads generally).
- Schudson's [-@schudsonGoodCitizenHistory1998] **"monitorial citizen"**: most people don't need to be, and aren't, constantly informed — they pay attention when something big happens. This isn't a democratic failure so much as a realistic description of busy lives.

## Mobilisation and demobilisation {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Mobilising** your own supporters is usually easier than persuading the undecided — and increasingly important as elections narrow to a small swing bloc.

- Facebook's 2010/2012 **"I voted" button experiments**: social pressure from friends significantly increased turnout — at platform scale, and with no public oversight of the experiment.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Demobilising opponents** is a parallel strategy:

- Merkel's CDU: campaigns deliberately made **boring**, to avoid mobilising the other side.
- **Negative campaigning**: evidence is mixed on whether it demobilises or backfires.
- Extreme case: delegitimising the *election itself* — Kligler-Vilenchik et al.'s [-@kliglerMobilizationDemobilizationDiscourses2021] Jerusalem study found a Palestinian Twittersphere segment framing voting as "betrayal of one's collective identity."
:::
:::

# Reading: Heiss & Matthes (2019)

## Leg 2: the participation paradox {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Heiss & Matthes [-@heissMatthesDoesIncidental2019], *New Media & Society* 21(11–12).

- The chapter says platforms lower the cost of participation. This paper asks the sharper question: **for whom?**
- **RQ**: Does incidental exposure to political information on social media *equalise* the participation gap between politically interested and disinterested people — or *reinforce* it?
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### "Incidental exposure"
Coming across political content **without searching for it** — a friend's share, a "liked" news page turning up in your feed — as opposed to deliberately seeking out political information.
:::
:::
:::

## Two competing hypotheses {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Equalising hypothesis**

- Low-interest people wouldn't otherwise see *any* political content.
- Even brief, incidental encounters can be liked/shared cheaply, potentially building future engagement.
- Content shared by trusted friends may carry more weight than content from an outlet you'd never have sought out.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reinforcing hypothesis**

- High-interest people follow *more* political sources — so they get incidentally exposed *more often* too.
- Only people who already care are likely to **systematically process** and act on what they encounter.
- Low-interest people may find unwanted political content annoying (**reactance**) or feel less capable next to politically active friends (**negative social comparison**) — actively discouraging participation.
:::
:::

## The design {.smaller}

- **Two-wave online panel**, Austria, around the **2017 national election** (N = 559; representative quotas for age, gender, education).
- Wave 1: 29 Aug–2 Sep 2017. Wave 2: 5–12 Oct 2017 — **one month of intensive campaigning** between waves.
- **Incidental exposure** measured at Wave 1: "How often are you accidentally exposed to political posts in your social media newsfeed without having actively searched for or intentionally included such information?" (1 = never, 7 = often).
- **Political interest** measured at Wave 1 (interest in politics + the election).
- Digital participation split into **low-effort** (liking/sharing, brief comments, signing an online petition) and **high-effort** (writing a substantive comment, contacting a politician/journalist, creating a political group) — measured at *both* waves.

## Why split low- vs high-effort participation? {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
### The paper's hypothesis, going in
Incidental exposure will have a **more pronounced effect on low-effort than high-effort participation** — because incidental content tends to get only shallow (implicit/heuristic) processing, and high-effort activities need the kind of deliberate, systematic processing that requires actually caring.
:::

This directly refines the textbook's "platforms lower the cost of participation" claim: **which** kind of participation, and lowered for **whom**, are separate empirical questions — not a single effect.

## Findings 1: low-effort participation {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Incidental exposure has a clear **positive main effect** on low-effort participation in both the cross-sectional and (more robust) panel models.
- Critically, this effect is **not conditional on political interest** — it boosts low-effort activity **roughly equally**, whether someone is highly engaged or not.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-tip}
### So far, equalising?
Low-cost activities (liking, sharing, signing a petition) can be done almost reflexively, on heuristic cues like emotional content — so *this part* of the story looks consistent with the optimistic, equalising view.
:::
:::
:::

## Findings 2: high-effort participation — the twist {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
### Against the equalising hypothesis
For **high-effort participation**, the panel model shows incidental exposure has **no positive effect for anyone** — and a **significant negative effect for people with low political interest**. For the highly interested, the effect trends positive but doesn't reach significance.
:::

- In plain terms: incidentally stumbling on political content on your feed does **not** turn a disengaged person into someone who writes substantive comments or contacts a politician — if anything, it seems to actively **suppress** that kind of costly participation for them.
- The gap in high-effort participation between high- and low-interest people, if anything, **widens**.

## Why would incidental exposure backfire for the disengaged? {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Shallow processing**: incidental content is processed implicitly/heuristically — enough to prompt a quick like, not enough to build the motivation for costly action.
- **Psychological reactance**: politically disengaged people may find unwanted, unsought political content annoying — repeated unwanted exposure can produce a negative reaction rather than engagement.
- **Negative social comparison**: seeing politically sophisticated friends' posts may make less-engaged people feel *less* capable and *less* politically efficacious — lowering, not raising, their willingness to participate.
- The authors could not fully adjudicate between these mechanisms with survey data alone — flagged as a direction for future (experimental) research.
:::

## The bottom line {.smaller}

::: {.callout-important}
### RQ answered
Incidental exposure on social media **reinforces**, rather than equalises, the participation gap that matters most — costly, high-effort political participation. It does lift *low-effort* activity for everyone roughly equally, but that is not the kind of participation classical democratic theory cares most about.
:::

- This directly **replicates-and-overturns** Valeriani & Vaccari's [-@valerianiVaccariAccidentalExposure2016] earlier, cross-sectional finding of an equalising effect — Heiss & Matthes's own cross-sectional model reproduces that result, but it **does not survive** the switch to panel data, which better handles reverse causation and selection.

## Not just Austria: the gap at home {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: setup-aes
#| include: false
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

aes_path <- "data/Australian Election Study, 1987-2022 Trends.xlsx"
aes_raw <- read_excel(aes_path, sheet = "5.4", col_names = FALSE)
aes_years <- as.numeric(unlist(aes_raw[2, 3:11]))

# item label carries down every row (rows 3-53); breakdown label is NA for
# the "Total" rows and filled for Gender/Age/Education/Vote sub-groups
aes_dat <- aes_raw[3:53, ] |>
  setNames(c("item", "breakdown", as.character(aes_years))) |>
  mutate(breakdown = ifelse(is.na(breakdown), "Total", breakdown)) |>
  filter(item == "Taken part in a protest") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = as.character(aes_years), names_to = "year", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) |>
  filter(!is.na(pct))

brand_blue <- "#0148A4"
brand_red <- "#e64626"
brand_charcoal <- "#424242"

aes_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = brand_charcoal),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = brand_charcoal),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = brand_charcoal, size = 14)
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
### The Australian Election Study, 1987–2022
The AES asks Australians every election whether they've **taken part in a protest** in the past five years — tracked here across 35 years and nine elections.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-aes-education
#| fig-cap: "Protest participation by education, 1987–2022 (AES)"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4
educ_dat <- aes_dat |>
  filter(breakdown %in% c(
    "Education: No qualification",
    "Education: Non-tertiary qualification",
    "Education: Tertiary qualification"
  )) |>
  mutate(breakdown = recode(breakdown,
    "Education: No qualification" = "No qualification",
    "Education: Non-tertiary qualification" = "Non-tertiary",
    "Education: Tertiary qualification" = "Tertiary"
  ))
educ_dat$breakdown <- factor(educ_dat$breakdown, levels = c("No qualification", "Non-tertiary", "Tertiary"))

ggplot(educ_dat, aes(x = year, y = pct, colour = breakdown)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "No qualification" = "#A9C6E8",
    "Non-tertiary" = brand_blue,
    "Tertiary" = "#002B5C"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = aes_years) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% participated in past 5 years", title = "By education") +
  aes_theme
```
:::

## Context: who's at university? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-highered-gender
#| fig-cap: "Commencing domestic higher education students by gender, 2015–2024"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
highered_dat <- readr::read_csv("data/aes-commencing-highered-gender-2015-2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(Other = `Indeterminate/intersex/other`) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Females, Males, Other), names_to = "gender", values_to = "n") |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
highered_dat$gender <- factor(highered_dat$gender, levels = c("Females", "Males", "Other"))

ggplot(highered_dat, aes(x = Year, y = pct, colour = gender)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Females" = brand_red, "Males" = brand_blue, "Other" = "#FFB800")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(highered_dat$Year)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of commencing students", title = "Commencing higher ed students, by gender") +
  aes_theme
```

## What does each group's media diet look like, among younger voters? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-media-diet
#| fig-cap: "Media diet composition for following the 2025 election, ages 18-40, by education (AES 2025)"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
aes2025 <- read.csv("data/AES2025_general.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(aes2025)[1] <- "id"

media2025_dat <- aes2025 |>
  filter(AGE >= 18, AGE < 40, G3_EDU %in% c(1, 2)) |>
  mutate(edu = ifelse(G3_EDU == 1, "Higher education", "Non-higher education")) |>
  select(edu, A2_1, A2_2, A2_3, A2_4) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = A2_1:A2_4, names_to = "item", values_to = "val") |>
  filter(val %in% 1:4) |>
  mutate(
    # A2 is coded 1 = "a good deal" ... 4 = "none at all"; invert to an
    # attention score (0-3, higher = more attention) before averaging
    score = 4 - val,
    item = recode(item, A2_1 = "Newspapers", A2_2 = "Television", A2_3 = "Radio", A2_4 = "Internet")
  ) |>
  group_by(edu, item) |>
  summarise(mean_score = mean(score), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(edu) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * mean_score / sum(mean_score)) |>
  ungroup()

media2025_dat$item <- factor(media2025_dat$item, levels = c("Internet", "Newspapers", "Radio", "Television"))

ggplot(media2025_dat, aes(x = edu, y = share, fill = item)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(share), "%"), colour = item),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 4.5, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Television" = "#A9C6E8",
    "Radio" = "#FFB800",
    "Newspapers" = brand_charcoal,
    "Internet" = brand_red
  )) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Television" = brand_charcoal,
    "Radio" = brand_charcoal,
    "Newspapers" = "white",
    "Internet" = "white"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of media diet") +
  aes_theme
```

::: {.footer}
Australian Election Study 2025 (general release), ages 18–40 (n = 499). Attention to the campaign via each medium (A2), by university-level education (G3_EDU).
:::

## Reading the 2025 media-diet chart {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Pooled across ages 18–40, both groups' diets are **internet-led**: 39% for higher education, 41% for non-higher education — no education gap in flagship medium, if anything a slight reversal.
- Television is a stable second for both (26% vs 29%).
- Newspapers are the clearest point of difference: **16% for higher education vs 13% for non-higher education** — the one medium where graduates lean in more, though it's still the smallest slice for both.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Across every age cut we've tried — under-45, under-30, four 5-year bands, and now the full 18–40 pool — the story doesn't change: education does not predict *which* medium dominates a younger Australian's media diet. It may predict *whether* they turn that diet into political action (the AES protest-participation gap earlier this week), but not the composition of the diet itself.
:::

## In-class activity 4 {.smaller}

::: {.center}

Heiss & Matthes suggest that being incidentally exposed to friends' sophisticated political posts might make less-engaged people feel *less* capable, not more — and so participate *less*, not more.

# Where this leaves the verdict

## Bringing the week together {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Platforms genuinely **lower the cost** of some political actions — that part of the "platforms democratise participation" story is real, for low-effort activity.
- But the **high-effort participation that most shapes political voice** — writing, organising, contacting decision-makers — is **not** equalised by incidental exposure. If anything, the gap between interested and disinterested citizens **widens**.
- This is **Leg 2** of the semester's argument: platforms don't uniformly weaken *or* strengthen democratic participation — they **change its texture**, making cheap participation abundant while leaving (or worsening) the deeper inequality in who does the costly, consequential kind.
- Connects to **Week 3**'s Leg 1: just as algorithmic gatekeeping is invisible and unaccountable, the participation gap here is also largely **invisible** — it looks like "everyone's engaging," because everyone likes and shares, while the substantive gap hides underneath.
:::

## Where this connects forward {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Week 8** — movements (Ch 8): **Leg 3**, Internet capital vs. social capital — does *collective*, movement-level organising bypass the individual participation gap we saw today?
- **Week 9** — governance: could platform design changes (not just individual behaviour) narrow the high-effort participation gap?
- **Week 12** — entertainment/politainment: another "low-effort, high-reach" channel — does it suffer the same reinforcing dynamic?
- **Week 13** — the verdict: participation looks more abundant in the platform era, but is it more *equal*? Today's evidence says no.
:::

## Key takeaways {.smaller}

- The **four ages of campaigning** (party-, mass-media-, target-group-, individual-centred) accumulate rather than replace one another; platforms intensify the most recent, **data-driven, personalised** era.
- Platforms rarely **decide** election outcomes alone — structural factors (economy, incumbency, party coalitions) matter as much or more; digital tools can equalise *and* reinforce existing resource advantages, depending on who has the skills and money to use them well.
- Campaign strategies on platforms: mostly **broadcasting over interaction**; persuasion works mainly on the margins (salience, not identity); mobilisation (turnout, social pressure) and demobilisation (boring campaigns, negative ads, delegitimising elections) are both platform-amplified.
- **Heiss & Matthes**: incidental exposure boosts **low-effort** participation for everyone roughly equally, but has **no positive — and for the disengaged, a negative — effect on high-effort participation**. The participation gap that matters most is **reinforced**, not closed.
